exampleAnswers.title: Solving Exponential Equations Containing Different Bases by Rewriting One Exponent

question.text: Find the value of $x$ that satisfies the equation $27^{x+2}=3^{4x}.$
question.explanation:
To solve this equation, we need both exponential terms to have a common base.

To do this, we write $27$ as $3^3,$ and then rewrite the left-hand side using the power rule of exponents:

\begin{align*} 27^{x+2} & =3^{4x} \\[3pt] \left(3^3\right)^{x+2} & =3^{4x} \\[3pt] 3^{3(x+2)} & =3^{4x} \end{align*}

Now, since both sides of the equation share the same base $(3)$, we equate the exponents and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} 3(x+2) & = 4x \\[3pt] 3x+6 & = 4x \\[3pt] x & = 6 \end{align*}

example.title: Solving Exponential Equations Containing Different Bases by Rewriting One Exponent

question.explanation:
To solve this equation, we need both exponential terms to have a common base.

To do this, we write $125$ as $5^3,$ and then rewrite the right-hand side using the power rule of exponents:

\begin{align*} 5^{m-10} &= 125^m\\[3pt] 5^{m-10} &= \left(5^3\right)^m\\[3pt] 5^{m-10} &= 5^{3m}\\[3pt] \end{align*}

Now, since both sides of the equation share the same base $(5)$, we equate the exponents and solve for $m\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} m-10 &= 3m \\[3pt] -2m &= 10 \\[3pt] m &= -5 \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Solving Exponential Equations Containing Different Bases by Rewriting Two Exponents

question.explanation:
To solve this equation, we need both exponential terms to have a common base. To do this, we rewrite the equation using $9=3^2$ and $27 = 3^3,$ as follows:

\[ \left(3^2\right)^{y}=\left(3^3\right)^{y-3} \]

Then, we apply the power rule of exponents. This gives:

\begin{align*} 3^{2y} = 3^{3(y-3)} \end{align*}

Now, since both sides of the equation share the same base $(3)$, we equate the exponents and solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} 2y &= 3(y-3)\\[3pt] 2y &= 3y-9 \\[3pt] y&=9 \end{align*}

example.title: Solving Exponential Equations Containing Different Bases by Rewriting Two Exponents

question.explanation:
To solve this equation, we need both exponential terms to have a common base. To do this, we rewrite the equation using $16=2^4$ and $8 = 2^3,$ as follows:

\[ \left(2^4\right)^{2n} = \left(2^3\right)^{n + 1} \\ \]

Then, we apply the power rule of exponents. This gives:

\begin{align*} 2^{8n} &= 2^{3(n + 1)} \\ \end{align*}

Now, since both sides of the equation share the same base $(2)$, we equate the exponents and solve for $n\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} 8n &= 3(n + 1) \\[3pt] 8n &= 3n + 3 \\[3pt] 5n &= 3 \\[3pt] n &= \dfrac 3 5 \end{align*}
